system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:a13ac2eb4a9e",
  "problem": "Whether to treat open-ended explanation training as a success given weak and mixed results on two evaluation metrics.",
  "did": "They reported the mixed results in the appendix, argued both metrics may understate learning, and treated an LLM-judge correctness measure as only preliminary because it is circular.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "directly judging explanation correctness with an LLM judge"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The hint setting is a large distribution shift, simulatability depends on simulator capability, and the LLM-judge evaluation is circular since training and evaluation come from the same pipeline."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:57fb5cc4225a",
  "problem": "Choosing which LLM should power the auditing agent and how to compare candidate models fairly.",
  "did": "They compared Claude Sonnet 4, o3 and Qwen 2.5 72b using the simple D + M configuration with 20 audits per fine-tune, weighing false positives alongside detection.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Qwen 2.5 72b",
   "o3"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "D + M provides a simple configuration for comparison across models, and minimizing false positives is equally important as detection."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:102292145a35",
  "problem": "Whether benchmark contamination from published breaks of some included defenses undermines the results.",
  "did": "The authors judged contamination not a major concern after noting low success rates and testing with the previously written attack paper placed in context.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "treating contamination as a major threat to validity"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Success rates were very low even for the best agent, and giving the model the attack paper did not significantly improve success."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:d0cb84656fbb",
  "problem": "How to filter the backdoor transfer data so that it carries the teacher's signal",
  "did": "Removed answers the unfinetuned model would produce identically. Kept the 50% of answers with the largest teacher-versus-base log-likelihood difference.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To keep the answers most characteristic of the teacher."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:572c442292c0",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim IP's general effectiveness given mixed results on compliance with explicit harmful requests.",
  "did": "They reported in the limitations that IP increased tendency to follow undesired instructions in two of six models and that it may make the model easier to misuse, rather than claiming uniform safety.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "In two out of six models tested, IP increased the tendency to follow instructions requesting the undesired behavior (e.g. Qwen 2.5 base)."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:1be7b75f55b5",
  "problem": "Whether to continue analyzing the defense after it was modified again by the authors after the first release.",
  "did": "Continued the work: attacked the third code release using the authors' pretrained CIFAR-10 model and updated the paper, as promised in the original disclaimer.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The first version promised to analyze future modifications once the authors provided a pretrained model."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:24b5ec49b091",
  "problem": "Whether baseliners should be allowed internet access when some tasks could be trivialized by external resources.",
  "did": "They always permitted web access to baseliners but banned AI assistants, Wolfram Alpha, and sign-in services.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "restricting internet access for baseliners"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Pilot studies showed significantly reduced human performance without web access, often from small hindrances like forgetting syntax."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:a820806bfca9",
  "problem": "Whether to continue investing in optimizing the baseline detection methods or to keep them as unoptimized baselines.",
  "did": "They left the detection methods unoptimized and did not try to fix all identified problems.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "optimizing the detection methods to maximize detector performance"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The goal was to provide an evaluation testbed rather than to maximize detector performance."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:816e585bbdc1",
  "problem": "Which attack scenarios to implement as proofs-of-concept versus leave as speculation.",
  "did": "They implemented realistic ethical proofs-of-concept in Section 3 and relegated attacks lacking a realistic, ethical test method to Section 4 as unvalidated discussion.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "implementing every attack vector"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "They could not easily identify a method for a realistic and ethical proof-of-concept for those attacks."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:faf4a2f358d2",
  "problem": "Whether IP makes models more likely to produce unwanted or harmful outputs when explicitly requested, a possible side effect of training with such instructions.",
  "did": "They evaluated IP-trained models using the inoculation prompt as the evaluation prompt and also ran Strong Reject for broader harmful compliance.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "To test whether IP increases compliance with unwanted requests compared to models trained without IP."
 }
]
